title: Be To and Be About To: Formal Arrangements and Imminence
summary: Use be to + infinitive for official future arrangements and formal instructions, including passive forms, while respecting its usual restriction to controllable future events. Use if ... is to ... for a required condition and be about to for something expected very soon.
learningObjectives: Recognise be to + infinitive in official announcements, formal arrangements and instructions, including prohibitions and passive directives.
Distinguish controllable, planned events from uncontrolled future developments, where be to is not normally used in this sense.
Use if + be to + infinitive to express an intended result that depends on meeting a necessary condition.
Use be about to + infinitive for imminent events and understand was/were about to as imminent future viewed from a past moment.

explanation.heading: Be to in official notices and news reporting
explanation.body: Present forms of be to + infinitive often introduce a scheduled action or announced plan in formal news reporting. They typically describe an event expected soon and organised by an authority or someone able to arrange it. The corresponding passive, be to be + past participle, puts attention on the event or object rather than its organiser. This use is different in tone from everyday be going to.
explanation.example: The visiting committee is to inspect the new centre on Thursday, and the final report is to be published on Friday.

explanation.heading: Be to for instructions, duties and prohibitions
explanation.body: Be to can also state a formal instruction, obligation or order, rather than simply predict the future. Negative forms such as are not to enter express prohibition. Passive instructions can be more impersonal because they omit the person expected to carry out the action. Always use the base infinitive after to, not an -ing verb.
explanation.example: Participants are to wear identification badges, and confidential documents are not to be removed from the building.

explanation.heading: Why controllability matters in future be to
explanation.body: For future reporting of official arrangements, be to normally refers to events that people can plan, authorise or control. It is not the neutral choice for naturally occurring or inherently unpredictable events with no organising agent, such as an unexpected meteor or the future spread of an illness. Will, may or other suitable forms are ordinarily used for such predictions. This restriction does not necessarily apply in the same way to was/were to when narrating later events from a past viewpoint.
explanation.example: The new bridge is to open in June, but nobody knows when the next strong earthquake will occur.

explanation.heading: If something is to happen: necessary conditions
explanation.body: In an if-clause, be to + infinitive can name a desired outcome whose achievement requires the action in the main clause. Compare this with present simple in an if-clause, where the condition is more typically the cause or event that triggers the main-clause consequence. Be to may also appear in a passive form for outcomes that must be achieved. Pay attention to the direction of dependence rather than treating the two structures as interchangeable.
explanation.example: If the exhibition is to open in May, the curators must approve the displays this week. If the exhibition opens in May, the town will attract more visitors.

explanation.heading: Be about to for an event on the verge of happening
explanation.body: Be about to + infinitive presents an event as expected almost immediately; it does not merely mean that something is planned at an unspecified later date. It is common in ordinary conversation and can be used in negatives. Was/were about to describes an event that seemed imminent at a moment in the past; whether it actually happened must be established by the context.
explanation.example: We are about to begin the meeting. Yesterday I was about to leave when the fire alarm sounded.

comparisons.title: An announced human arrangement versus an uncontrolled prediction

left.label: Be to: controllable official event
left.example: The council is to vote on the proposal tomorrow.
left.note: People can schedule the vote and the phrasing suits official reporting.

right.label: Will: uncontrolled event
right.example: The next volcanic eruption will happen at an unknown time.
right.note: No authority can schedule an eruption; be to is inappropriate as a simple forecast.

comparisons.title: A necessary condition versus a conditional consequence

left.label: If ... is to: an intended outcome
left.example: If the charity is to expand, it needs more volunteers.
left.note: Recruiting volunteers is necessary to achieve the expansion.

right.label: If + present simple: a triggering event
right.example: If the charity expands, it will need more volunteers.
right.note: Expansion is the condition that produces the future need.

examples.sentence: The education minister is to meet representatives from regional colleges tomorrow.
examples.note: Is to meet presents an organised official engagement.

examples.sentence: All laboratory visitors are to follow the posted safety instructions.
examples.note: Are to follow is a formal directive.

examples.sentence: The old stairway is to be repaired before the public reopening.
examples.note: The passive form presents a formally arranged action without naming the contractor.

examples.sentence: If the online archive is to remain accessible, the servers must be maintained regularly.
examples.note: Is to remain introduces a desired condition that requires preventive action.

examples.sentence: The speaker was about to announce the result when the lights went out.
examples.note: Was about to marks a past moment just before an anticipated announcement.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The visitors are to wearing protective glasses.
commonMistakes.correct: The visitors are to wear protective glasses.
commonMistakes.why: Be to takes a bare verb after the infinitive marker to, not an -ing form.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The damaged equipment is to replaced by Friday.
commonMistakes.correct: The damaged equipment is to be replaced by Friday.
commonMistakes.why: The passive be to construction needs to be followed by a past participle.

commonMistakes.incorrect: If the exhibition is succeed, the organisers need additional funding.
commonMistakes.correct: If the exhibition is to succeed, the organisers need additional funding.
commonMistakes.why: The goal-focused condition requires is to + base infinitive.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The lecture is about begin; please take your seats.
commonMistakes.correct: The lecture is about to begin; please take your seats.
commonMistakes.why: Imminence is expressed with be about to + base verb.

studyTips: Rewrite a formal notice using be to, then paraphrase it as an ordinary future statement and note the difference in register.
Build paired if-sentences: If the project is to succeed, ... and If the project succeeds, ...; explain which clause expresses the goal and which expresses its consequence.
Sort future events into controllable arrangements, uncontrolled predictions and imminent actions before deciding between be to, will and be about to.

exercises.prompt: A government notice announces a scheduled inspection. “The committee ___ the site on Friday.” Choose the formal future construction.
choices: is to inspect
is inspecting to
to be inspecting
exercises.feedback: Is to inspect expresses the officially arranged visit.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correctly formed formal prohibition for visitors.
choices: Visitors are not to entering the restricted room.
Visitors are not to enter the restricted room.
Visitors are not enter the restricted room.
exercises.feedback: Are not to enter is the correct prohibition, using to + base infinitive.

exercises.prompt: A scientist cannot predict when the next naturally occurring earthquake will happen. Choose the suitable sentence.
choices: The earthquake is to occurring next year.
The earthquake are to occur next year.
An earthquake may occur, but its timing is unknown.
exercises.feedback: May occur allows an uncontrolled uncertain event; be to is not a neutral schedule-like prediction here.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence correctly expresses a condition needed to achieve a goal?
choices: If the programme is to survive, it must attract new supporters.
If the programme is survive, it must attract new supporters.
If the programme to survive, it must attract new supporters.
exercises.feedback: Is to survive names the desired result; recruiting supporters is the necessary condition.

exercises.prompt: The official programme states that the delegates ___ (meet) the director on Wednesday. Write the be to verb phrase.
exercises.feedback: Are to meet announces an arranged official meeting.

exercises.prompt: The council has approved the work. “The bridge ___ (repair) next month.” Write the complete passive be to verb phrase.
exercises.feedback: Is to be repaired is the passive form for an officially authorised action.

exercises.prompt: The doors are opening in a moment. “We ___ (start) the presentation.” Write the complete be about to phrase.
exercises.feedback: Are about to start places the beginning in the immediate future.

exercises.prompt: Complete the goal-focused condition: “If the community garden ___ (succeed), local residents must keep volunteering.” Use be to.
exercises.feedback: Is to succeed presents success as the outcome that depends on volunteering.

exercises.prompt: Correct the official plan: “The committee are to inspecting the exhibition on Tuesday.”
acceptedAnswers: The committee are to inspect the exhibition on Tuesday.
exercises.feedback: To inspect uses the base infinitive, not inspecting. The plural collective agreement here is grammatical in British English.

exercises.prompt: Correct the impersonal instruction: “Confidential files are not to remove from the office.”
acceptedAnswers: Confidential files are not to be removed from the office.
exercises.feedback: An impersonal passive prohibition requires are not to be removed.

exercises.prompt: Correct the condition, preserving the intended outcome: “If the team is win the award, it must submit its work by Friday.”
acceptedAnswers: If the team is to win the award, it must submit its work by Friday.
exercises.feedback: If the team is to win expresses the goal that depends on submitting work.

exercises.prompt: Correct the imminent future expression: “The train is about leaving, so please board now.”
acceptedAnswers: The train is about to leave, so please board now.
exercises.feedback: Be about to + infinitive expresses imminent departure.

speakingExercises.prompt: Present the official arrangement. Facts: The panel / interview / candidates / on Monday. Use be to and full forms.
acceptedAnswers: The panel is to interview candidates on Monday.
speakingExercises.feedback: Is to interview conveys an official planned event.

speakingExercises.prompt: Give an official prohibition. Facts: Visitors / not / touch / the exhibits. Use be to with full forms.
acceptedAnswers: Visitors are not to touch the exhibits.
speakingExercises.feedback: Are not to touch is a formal negative instruction.

speakingExercises.prompt: Give the passive formal arrangement. Facts: The new entrance / open / next month. Use is to be + past participle.
acceptedAnswers: The new entrance is to be opened next month.
speakingExercises.feedback: Is to be opened announces an arranged event in passive form.

speakingExercises.prompt: Express a necessary condition for a goal. Facts: If / the project / succeed / we / need / more funding. Use is to in the if-clause and present simple in the main clause.
acceptedAnswers: If the project is to succeed, we need more funding.
speakingExercises.feedback: Is to succeed names the desired outcome for which funding is needed.

speakingExercises.prompt: Announce that a meeting will start in a moment. Facts: We / begin / the meeting. Use be about to.
acceptedAnswers: We are about to begin the meeting.
speakingExercises.feedback: Are about to begin expresses immediate imminence.

speakingExercises.prompt: Explain a past near-action. Facts: I / leave / when you called. Use was about to.
acceptedAnswers: I was about to leave when you called.
speakingExercises.feedback: Was about to places an imminent action at a moment in the past.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct aloud this official instruction: “All participants are to wearing safety helmets.”
acceptedAnswers: All participants are to wear safety helmets.
speakingExercises.feedback: Be to requires the base infinitive wear.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say two statements in this order, using full forms. Official plan: The mayor / visit / the library / tomorrow. Immediate event: The ceremony / start / now.
acceptedAnswers: The mayor is to visit the library tomorrow. The ceremony is about to start now.
speakingExercises.feedback: Is to visit conveys an official arrangement; is about to start conveys imminence.

listeningExercises.audioText: According to the official announcement, the transport minister is to visit the new terminal on Thursday. The visit has been arranged by the ministry.
choices: An unplanned natural event.
A visit already completed last Thursday.
An officially arranged future visit.
listeningExercises.feedback: Is to visit reports a scheduled engagement controlled by the ministry.

listeningExercises.audioText: Visitors are not to open the storage cabinets. Only authorised staff may handle the materials inside.
choices: They must leave the storage cabinets closed.
They are expected to inspect the cabinets themselves.
They may remove materials without permission.
listeningExercises.feedback: Are not to open states a formal prohibition.

listeningExercises.audioText: The approved renovation plan says the entrance is to be widened before November.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the four-word passive verb phrase immediately after “entrance”.
listeningExercises.feedback: Is to be widened is the spoken passive be to expression.

listeningExercises.audioText: Scientists can estimate volcanic activity, but nobody has organised an eruption for next month. They say another eruption may happen one day.
listeningExercises.prompt: Why does the speaker use may happen rather than a formal scheduled future?
choices: A mayor has ordered the eruption.
The event cannot be arranged by people.
The eruption was finished last month.
listeningExercises.feedback: A naturally occurring eruption is not a human-controlled scheduled event.

listeningExercises.audioText: If the youth orchestra is to perform at the festival, its members must practise the new pieces throughout the winter.
listeningExercises.prompt: What is the purpose of the winter practice?
choices: To cancel a completed concert.
To avoid purchasing new instruments.
To make the intended festival performance possible.
listeningExercises.feedback: Is to perform names the goal; practice is necessary to achieve it.

listeningExercises.audioText: The auditorium doors are closing and the lights are dimming. We are about to begin the film screening.
listeningExercises.prompt: When is the screening expected to begin?
choices: Almost immediately.
At an unspecified date next year.
At some time in the distant past.
listeningExercises.feedback: Are about to begin means the screening is imminent.

listeningExercises.audioText: The headteacher has issued a formal order. Students are to remain inside until the alarm ends.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the three-word verb phrase immediately after “Students”.
listeningExercises.feedback: Are to remain gives an official instruction in exactly the words heard.

listeningExercises.audioText: I was about to close the office when the delivery driver arrived.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the four-word verb phrase immediately after “I”.
listeningExercises.feedback: Was about to close describes what the speaker was on the point of doing.
